articles.description: The official in charge of President  Trump's ceasefire plan for Gaza criticized Israel for its attacks on the Palestinian territory and warned that the alternative to the U.S. proposal is the next war.
articles.title: Official leading Trump's Gaza ceasefire effort criticizes Israel for its attacks

articles.author: Elizabeth Blair
articles.description: The Japanese artist has died at age 97. Kusama's polka dotted pumpkins, "Infinity Rooms," and other repetitive and dreamlike artworks have been shown in museums and galleries worldwide.
articles.title: Yayoi Kusama, high priestess of polka dots, has died

articles.author: Sydney Lupkin
articles.description: The Bridge program, which began July 1, makes some Medicare beneficiaries eligible for obesity drugs for $50 a month. CVS and Walgreens say they've each already filled 100,000 such prescriptions.
articles.title: Drugstores say Medicare's $50 obesity drug program is catching on

articles.author: Vanessa Romo
articles.description: Since taking over in March, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has pivoted from the confrontational style of immigration enforcement of his predecessor, Kristi Noem. The latest data is reflective of a strategy that is working
articles.title: Immigration arrests soar, hitting 50,000 in July

articles.author: Jane Arraf
articles.description: Pilgrims came to Iraq from all over the world in August. Many Iraqi and Iranian pilgrims walked hundreds of miles in extreme heat to mark the event. Outside the shrines, the atmosphere is almost festive.
articles.title: Greetings from Karbala, Iraq, where millions gathered for a Shia pilgrimage

articles.author: Alex Olgin
articles.description: Indiana is the latest state to experiment with limiting what hospitals can charge, to try to get a handle on high health costs.
articles.title: States try new tactics to bring down high hospital prices

articles.author: Hansi Lo Wang
articles.description: A federal judge in Boston canceled a nationwide ruling that blocked U.S. Postal Service work on President Trump's order to limit mail-in voting for the midterm election. But a new block may come soon.
articles.title: Judge clears the way for Postal Service work on Trump's mail-in voting order for now

articles.author: Alice Woelfle
articles.description: Curry will be most remembered for his role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter, the tyrannical gender-bending alien scientist in both stage and screen versions of The Rocky Horror Picture Show. He was 80.
articles.title: Tim Curry, who defined 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show,' has died

articles.author: Joe Hernandez
articles.description: The proposal comes weeks before the midterm elections, when food prices and the cost of living are expected to be major issues on voters' minds.
articles.title: Will Trump's latest beef plan make your hamburger cheaper? Not much, experts say

articles.author: Terry Gross
articles.description: "I've always believed that a part of my magic, if there was any, was the fact that I look so artificial — but I am so totally real," Parton said in 2001.
articles.title: Dolly Parton lived her motto: 'More is more'

articles.author: Mabel Banfield-Nwachi (now) and Adam Fulton (earlier)
articles.description:
Foreign nationals from India, US, UK, Australia, Malaysia and Ukraine among those missing

Flash floods leave scores dead and hundreds missing

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

Eyewitness accounts have been emerging from the Tibetan side of the border, with a woman saying she was travelling from Gyirong town towards Nepal on Wednesday morning when her group encountered the flood about 4km from Gyirong port.
“Trees and electricity poles had already been knocked down, and the flood water was bearing down on us. We didn’t dare turn around, so we could only reverse,” the woman, surnamed Fang, told Xiaoxiang Morning News.
I was really scared. My whole body was trembling.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nepal flash flood live updates: 270 bodies recovered with hundreds more missing

articles.author: Ben Smee Queensland state correspondent
articles.description:
State government says ‘breach bail, go to jail’ laws raise risk of overcrowding in jails, while one expert warns they may lead to ‘cruel outcomes’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Queensland government’s latest law and order crackdown – subjecting some children as young as 10 to a mandatory sentence of a year behind bars – could lead to “cruel outcomes”, according to human rights lawyers.
In documents tabled with the legislation on Thursday, the government conceded its laws, dubbed “breach bail, go to jail”, would breach human rights and risk further straining the state’s overcrowded jails, youth detention centres and police watch houses.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Queensland concedes law imposing mandatory jail on some offenders as young as 10 breaches human rights

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose
articles.description:
Government measures to improve resilience are not due until 2030 and July’s  hack has not altered this timeline
 
Hundreds of Britain’s smallest power plants could remain at a higher risk to state-sponsored cyber-attacks until the 2030s despite a successful Iran-linked hack last month, it has emerged.
Officials this week briefed energy bosses on the breach, which is understood to have shut an unnamed small gas power plant for four days last month, and put the industry on alert over the growing cyber threat facing energy infrastructure.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK’s small power plants face continued cyber risk after Iran-linked hack

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Report shines light on ‘catastrophic situation’ where young people make themselves more ill to avoid losing support
Some of the most vulnerable children and young people in care are deliberately self-harming to avoid being abandoned when they get better or turn 18 and face a “cliff edge” of no further support, according to research.
Abi Booth, a psychotherapist who works with children and young people, said some were in a “catastrophic situation” in which they were hurting themselves to keep their place in therapeutic facilities.
In the UK, the youth suicide charity Papyrus can be contacted on 0800 068 4141 or email pat@papyrus-uk.org, and in the UK and Ireland Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is at 988 or chat for support. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Vulnerable children deliberately self-harming to stay in care, research finds

articles.author: Tom McIlroy Political editor
articles.description:
Prime minister intervenes amid anger at news Tony Burke was planning to cut intake of 20,000 arrivals by a third

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese has guaranteed Australia’s annual refugee intake will not be cut next financial year, shutting down plans for the arrivals quota to drop by one-third to Coalition-era levels.
Labor MPs and refugee advocates reacted angrily to news on Thursday morning that the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, was planning to cut intake of 20,000 arrivals to 13,750 in 2027-28.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Albanese vows refugee intake won’t be slashed after earlier reports of Coalition-level cut

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime
The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.
Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’

articles.author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
articles.description:
The once world-leading producer of crude oil has plunged into an energy crisis as Kyiv targets its refineries
A sanctioned shadow fleet tanker carries oil from Nato member Turkey to a Russian Baltic port. A deal is signed for Russian oil to be processed in Kazakhstan. Fuel cargoes arrive from India via Egypt. The Kremlin pressures allies to sell it badly needed fuel.
The data points may be diverse, but they point to a single inescapable conclusion.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ukraine’s drone attacks have left Russia desperately scrambling for oil imports

articles.author: Anne Davies
articles.description:
Former building commissioner David Chandler told inquiry of clashes with ‘loud and overbearing’ developer Jean Nassif

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A fugitive Sydney developer allegedly warned the then-New South Wales building commissioner that he would “harm” him if he got in the way of his projects which were being inspected for defects, the corruption watchdog has heard.
Giving evidence to the Independent Commission against Corruption on Thursday, David Chandler described an interaction he had with Toplace developments’ Jean Nassif.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘If you harm my project, I’ll harm you’: former NSW official tells Icac about fugitive developer’s call

articles.author: Kat Wong, Nino Bucci and Henry Belot
articles.description:
Nepali tour operator fears 15 Australians who had been on a trek near the border with China have died after devastating flood

Nepal flash flood live updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A New South Wales couple on a spiritual pilgrimage are among the first of 34 Australians identified as missing after flash flooding ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border.
Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife, Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were among 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash in Tibet on a spiritual trip, according to their son.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nepal floods: missing Australians identified as children as young as 11 among those yet to be found

articles.author: Achol Arok and Nick Visser
articles.description:
This blog is now closed

Nepal flash flood disaster – live updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says Dfat officials are ready to provide consular assistance to Australians in Nepal, after the devastating flooding in the country.
A local tourism official said they believed 34 Australians were missing in the area, among hundreds of foreign nationals. Australian officials were not confirming numbers at this stage, and were working to check on the welfare of people they know were in the affected region.
Australians in the affected area should follow the advice of local authorities. We are aware of a number of Australians in the area and Australian officials are urgently working to confirm their welfare. We are liaising with local authorities as well as tour operators.
We stand ready to provide consular assistance.
The images are very disturbing indeed. We do know that there are Australians in the area. We don’t know exactly how many.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pauline Hanson adds to confusion over One Nation’s immigration policy – as it happened

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
articles.description:
Rules will require hedge funds, insurers and pension firms to report all non-financial wrongdoing  
The City’s largest hedge funds, insurers and pension funds are racing to prepare for sweeping rules that will stop nearly 40,000 companies from hiding bullying and harassment cases from the financial watchdog.
From the start of next month, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will expand a crackdown on bad behaviour in the banking industry to a wider group of City investment firms and brokers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: City firms race to prepare for FCA crackdown on bullying and harassment

articles.author: Kate Lamb with Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi, and agencies
articles.description:
Entire villages swept away after glacial collapse triggers flood in mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

What we know so far

Have you been affected by the flash floods?

Nearly 1,500 people are missing, the majority of them tourists, authorities have said, after a catastrophic flash flood hit Nepal and Tibet, roaring down valleys and wiping out entire villages, with the preliminary death toll standing at 165.
Rescuers are racing to locate people missing in the mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims, including the hundreds of nationals from India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nearly 1,500 missing, mostly tourists, after Nepal-Tibet flash flood kills at least 165

articles.author: Sandra Laville Environment correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: utility company wants to draw off tens of millions of litres of water a day from Thames and replace it with treated effluent
Levels of a toxic “forever chemical” rose to 13 times the legal limit during Thames Water pilots for a controversial multimillion pound water recycling scheme that will pump millions of litres of treated sewage into the River Thames during drought.
The data from the pilots is in stark contrast to public comments from Thames Water that their water recycling project in south-west London will not harm the riverine environment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Forever chemicals’ surge during pilot of Thames Water plan to combat drought

articles.author: Helena Horton and George Francis Lee
articles.description:
Horticulturalists begin moving and propagating plants before the rusty and warped Palm House begins renovation – but some are too tall to save
It will be a gut-wrenching moment for the horticulturalists at Kew Gardens when some of the magnificent trees in the Palm House have to be felled.
“There are some sad moments ahead,” said Palm House manager, Will Spoelstra, who knows all the plants inside the cathedral-like greenhouse.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Sad moments ahead’: Kew Gardens to fell rare trees in race to save Victorian greenhouse

articles.author: Chris Osuh
articles.description:
Allegations Nathan Cofnas was unqualified for Ghent role and would cause ‘negative impact’ made to senior leaders months ago
Nathan Cofnas, the academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism, has been accused of having “very limited expertise” for his academic role by professors also working at Ghent University, who say he has a “far-right agenda”.
Cofnas secured a postdoctoral research role “on the future of liberalism” at Belgium’s Ghent University in March. Weeks later, Ghent’s department of philosophy and moral sciences handed a 19-page statement to university officials, setting out why it believed it was “improbable” that Cofnas was the best candidate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ghent professors challenged expertise of Jason Arday’s plagiarism accuser

articles.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
articles.description:
Comté, beaufort and abondance makers can temporarily supplement cows’ diets as there is ‘no grass left to eat’
Strict production rules will be loosened for some of France’s most famous cheeses after drought and repeated heatwaves dried out grazing pastures, threatening the livelihoods of traditional dairy workers.
Comté, a hard cheese made from raw cows’ milk in the Jura mountains, is France’s top-selling traditional cheese, with more than 62,000 tonnes produced last year. The government announced on Wednesday that its producers would be granted a temporary change to strict rules on grazing after farmers said extreme heat had scorched their pastures, putting production at risk.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: France to relax cheese production rules after drought takes toll on grazing land

articles.author: Tim Jonze and Sian Cain
articles.description:
From the 1950s to the 2020s, Kusama produced vivid paintings, sculptures and vast installations that often drew on her experience of hallucinations

Kusama – a life in pictures

Was Kusama the world’s favourite artist?

Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese outsider artist who reached superstar status after decades living in a psychiatric hospital, has died aged 97.
Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August, her company Yayoi Kusama Inc announced in a statement on Thursday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who became a global superstar, dies aged 97

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Sign up for the US Breaking News email

A US military strike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the Caribbean on Tuesday killed four people, officials said.
US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said in a post on X that the strike targeted a vessel “operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Democratic states sue to block postal service from carrying out Trump’s mail-in voting order – as it happened

articles.author: Press Association
articles.description:
Actor says she had the ‘weirdest six months of my life’, after being diagnosed days after her Dawson’s Creek co-star James Van Der Beek died of cancer
Busy Philipps has revealed she had a brain tumour removed, which was diagnosed shortly after her Dawson’s Creek co-star James Van Der Beek died from bowel cancer.
The 47-year-old, born Elizabeth Philipps, starred in the hit US teen drama as Audrey Liddell opposite Van Der Beek, who died in February aged 48 after being diagnosed with bowel cancer.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Busy Philipps reveals brain tumour diagnosis: ‘I’m grateful to be alive’

articles.author: Nick Robins-Early
articles.description:
Exclusive: Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said outcome ‘is not an all clear to say the product is safe’

Meta agrees to major changes to Facebook and Instagram in settlement

The star witness in the US government’s landmark trial against Meta believes that a multibillion-dollar settlement reached on Wednesday does not go far enough to stop the social media giant’s harms to young users.
“The limitations that are in the agreement are the equivalent of saying: ‘Well you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day,’” said whistleblower and ex-Facebook employee Arturo Béjar. “It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Key witness in Meta trial says terms of settlement insufficient to halt apps’ harms to teenagers

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Democrat Eric Hafner, to be released in 2036, also ran for seat in 2024, securing spot on that general election ballot
A man who is serving time in a federal prison in New York advanced on Wednesday from the primary for Alaska’s lone US House seat.
Eric Hafner, a registered Democrat, also ran for the seat in 2024 and secured a spot on the general election ballot that November despite a challenge brought by the Alaska Democratic party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man in prison in New York advances in primary for Alaska’s US House seat

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
Then House candidate joined Democratic Socialists of America in 2018 but didn’t renew membership after a year
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America after not renewing her membership for seven years, amid speculation that she might run for president in 2028.
The 36-year-old New York representative and one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists renewed her membership in the group’s national organization after reports emerged earlier this month that it had lapsed. Ocasio-Cortez initially joined the group in 2018.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez rejoins DSA after membership lapse of seven years

articles.author: Caroline Davies and Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
More than 400 travellers are said to be missing after flood on Tibet border, including 33 Britons

Flash floods on Nepal-Tibet border – latest updates

Thirty-three British citizens including a 13-year-old girl are among more than 400 travellers missing after a flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, according to Nepal’s tourism board.
The sudden flood happened on the Tibetan side of the Bhote Koshi River at about 8.30am local time on Wednesday. The 33 UK citizens are among at least 341 foreign nationals unaccounted for.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Girl, 13, among missing British citizens after flash flood in Nepal

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and agencies
articles.description:
At least 157 people dead and hundreds of tourists among missing after roads, bridges and power plants swept away

Nepal-Tibet flash floods – live updates

At least 157 people have been killed and hundreds, including large numbers of foreign tourists, are missing after flash floods ⁠hit the Himalayan border areas of ⁠Nepal and Tibet in China, police have said, with parts of India also at risk.
The disaster was caused by a torrent of mud, water and debris that burst from the banks of a river that runs between China and Nepal. Homes, roads, bridges and power plants were swept away in Nepal, ⁠while officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Flash floods on Nepal-Tibet border leave scores dead and hundreds missing

articles.author: Adam Gabbatt
articles.description:
The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans

This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday

Earlier this year, a survey found that Canada, along with Switzerland, was the best-liked country in the world. We all know this kind of polling is about as scientific as a high school popularity contest, but at least anecdotally, Canadians have a reputation for being friendly and welcoming, respectful and polite. Many people would find it difficult to dislike Canadians.
But not Donald Trump, who in a “hold my beer” moment this week demonstrated that he, at least, finds it easy to resent Canadians. The US president called the country “difficult and unreasonable”, and in a particularly hysterical moment, threatened to rename a lake, after trade talks collapsed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticks

articles.author: Sam Jones in Madrid
articles.description:
Albanian criminal has cut bars, descended sheets and even used human pyramid in escapes in Italy and Belgium
Police in Spain have arrested a dangerous Albanian criminal nicknamed the “escape wizard” who has managed to break out of four jails in Italy and Belgium by sawing through bars, clambering down knotted sheets and even using a human pyramid to breach prison walls.
The fugitive, who has not been officially named, was arrested after officers from the Policía Nacional force discovered he was living in the north-eastern Spanish city of Tarragona. He was the subject of a European arrest warrant issued by the Italian authorities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Escape wizard’ who has broken out of four prisons is arrested in Spain

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking
South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.
A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs

articles.author: Jon Henley
articles.description:
Lethal temperatures ​and wildfires have exposed a widening gulf between voters demanding ​action and politicians unwilling to confront the long-term choices global heating requires
• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
The climate crisis means “we’re going to have to change everything – the way we live, the way we produce, the way we trade,” France’s veteran radical-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, told the summer congress of his France Insoumise party last weekend.
The term “climate change”, said Mélenchon – the most likely rival to Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential run-off, according to one poll this week – may sound “almost reassuring”, but its actual impact will feel like “landing on another planet whenever we leave home”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock?

articles.author: Kat Lay Global health correspondent
articles.description:
The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected
A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?
Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?

articles.author: Seham Tantesh in Gaza, and Julian Borger
articles.description:
Efforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly cost
As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.
With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

articles.author: Lauren Aratani in New York
articles.description:
Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated

Are you a Canadian boycotting US products? We’d like to hear from you

Using the bathroom or having a cry is about to become more expensive for North Americans as the US and Canada enter a full-fledged trade war that threatens to flush away decades of peaceful trading between the two nations.
After trade negotiations broke down between the two countries last weekend, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, vowed to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar” and unveiled a list of nearly 900 American goods that will face 25% to 50% tariffs starting on 8 September.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada

articles.author: Kaamil Ahmed
articles.description:
In Ghana, a grassroots movement is championing nutritious, homegrown, climate-resilient produce, rather than western imports
After three years at catering school in Accra, Abiro Wisdom was certain of one thing – he did not want to go into catering. At least not the route that he might be expected to take. His course had prepared students for working in international hotels, focusing on French, Italian and Mexican cuisine. The nutritious, homegrown food that Wisdom had eaten while growing up in Bolgatanga, northern Ghana, did not feature at all.
“I didn’t see myself there,” he says of the big chain hotels. “I felt I wouldn’t be myself working there – I wouldn’t be able to talk about the food from where I come from.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Moringa lattes and tigernut kebabs: the Ghanaians ‘taking back the power’ of their food

articles.author: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad and Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Authorities at biggest state hospital in Islamabad say 15 babies were in the ward when fire broke out
At least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire that broke out in the maternity ward at one of Pakistan’s most prominent state hospitals.
The blaze began in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, the biggest state hospital in Islamabad.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: At least 14 newborn babies die in fire at Pakistan hospital’s maternity ward

articles.author: Deepa Parent
articles.description:
As photojournalist sentenced to 15 years, rights groups warn law would turn civic engagement into security crime
Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign media, in a move human rights groups have said attempts to “sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world”.
For journalists, researchers and even ordinary citizens, the proposed law being discussed by Iranian lawmakers this month could make speaking to international audiences and groups a potential criminal act and restrict coverage of events such as January’s mass anti-regime protests.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in ‘chilling’ crackdown

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Internal calls to end war get louder as Gulf neighbours plan alternative pipelines to cut reliance on waterway
Is the strait of Hormuz, recently cited by the office of the Iranian supreme leader as “the pillar of Iran’s new security order”, and as transformative as possessing a nuclear weapon, in reality becoming a fast-diminishing asset, leaving Iran increasingly vulnerable to the new planned US wave of economic sanctions?
It is the key debate that is raging inside Iran, with many different conclusions being drawn for Tehran’s negotiating strategy. Those who warn the strait’s value as a chokehold on the world economy will erode, leaving the country without foreign exchange reserves, argue that Iran’s negotiators should seek a deal soon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran faces strait of Hormuz paradox as strategic value of chokehold erodes

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Heavy rain expected in parts of Vietnam and southern ‌China, as another storm system, Typhoon Saudel, heads for Japan and Taiwan
Widespread flooding triggered by Typhoon Narra has submerged homes and forced mass evacuations in southern China, as another storm system tracked towards Japan and Taiwan.
Authorities in Chongzuo, in China’s Guangxi region – famous for its giant waterfalls and karst limestone mountains – on Tuesday evacuated more than 15,000 people after water ⁠levels surpassed a record high set in 2008.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Typhoon Narra: record flood waters submerge homes and force mass evacuations in China

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, deported to Honduras, is latest military spouse to face removal amid Trump 2.0
The wife of an active-duty US soldier was deported on Monday to her native Honduras, according to her family and the federal Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo is at least the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty US soldier to be deported under the immigration crackdown during Donald Trump’s second presidency.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wife of US soldier deported after Trump rollback on military family protections

articles.author: Associated Press in Port-au-Prince
articles.description:
Gang leader threatens to kill hostages after attack in Kenscoff in which homes were also set alight

‘A massacre’: Haiti gangs carrying out mass killings

At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped when armed men attacked a once peaceful community near Haiti’s capital at the weekend, the UN has said.
A gang leader has threatened to kill the hostages if authorities kill any gang members as they try to secure the community of Kenscoff, nestled in the hills above Port-au-Prince.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: At least 47 killed and dozens kidnapped in gang attack near Haiti capital

articles.author: Martin Belam
articles.description:
US president has been obsessed with restricting the ability to vote by mail, despite using it himself. Plus, why we are still fascinated with Meg from the White Stripes

Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it is unclear whether or not his administration will be able to take action before the midterm elections in November. The court’s justices voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction that a judge in Massachusetts had placed in June on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place, and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges.
Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own…
articles.title: Supreme court threatens midterms mail-in voting as it backs Trump plan | First Thing

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
The flagship environmental initiative has achieved ‘negligible’ results. Why so little progress, and what are the risks as the planet gets hotter? Plus, fusion dance pioneer Usha Jey
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The whitewashing of the Green India Mission forest expansion project

articles.author: Julian Borger Senior international correspondent
articles.description:
Washington launches campaign to isolate Tehran but it is unclear whether it will apply measures to China
The US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do.
It is unclear, however, how far the Trump administration is prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran

articles.author: Caroline Davies
articles.description:
Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy.
Prince Harry’s spokesperson confirmed he was no longer a trustee of African Parks, which admitted last year that human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in the Republic of the Congo.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Prince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abuses

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Test of US rhetoric will rest on whether nations such as India, China and Russia view economic threats as credible
Tehran has vowed to retaliate against any country that cooperates with the US attempt to impose fresh sanctions against Iran in what the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has billed as “the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary”.
In advance of the US announcement, the United Arab Emirates, Iran’s single biggest trading partner in the Middle East, announced it was ending all trade with Iran, a move Tehran believes was coordinated between Washington and the UAE.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran vows to retaliate against countries that cooperate with fresh US sanctions

articles.author: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad
articles.description:
Supreme court ordered transfer of ex-leader whose health is reportedly deteriorating, but he was returned to prison several hours later


 Pakistan’s jailed former prime minister Imran Khan was briefly taken to a hospital in the country’s capital on supreme court orders after weeks of uproar about his deteriorating health.
Khan, 73, was transferred to the hospital in the early hours of Friday, but then moved back to Adiala prison in Rawalpindi after a ⁠few hours, a spokesperson for his party said on Friday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jailed ex-Pakistan PM Imran Khan allowed brief hospital visit after uproar over health

articles.author: Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent
articles.description:
UK has refused resettlement application despite ‘years of loyal service’ that have resulted in ‘constant fear’ of reprisals
A man has received threats from the Taliban after his work for the Afghan police was revealed by a Ministry of Defence leak and the UK refused his application for resettlement.
Hamid* worked for the Afghan national police special unit and received certificates for his work signed by senior British figures praising his “dedication, unparalleled service and leadership”. His details were also included in an accidental 2022 leak by an MoD official that identified 18,700 Afghans who had worked with or for the British government.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Taliban threaten former Afghan police worker after MoD leak reveals identity

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Sign up for the US Breaking News email

A US military strike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the Caribbean on Tuesday killed four people, officials said.
US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said in a post on X that the strike targeted a vessel “operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Democratic states sue to block postal service from carrying out Trump’s mail-in voting order – as it happened

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Jes Staley told US House committee he also was at one point named a trustee of convicted sex offender’s estate
Former JPMorgan Chase executive Jes Staley told US lawmakers he repeatedly shared confidential and market-sensitive bank ⁠information with Jeffrey Epstein and ⁠was at one ​point named as a trustee of his estate, according to a transcript released by the House oversight committee on Wednesday.
These admissions come as lawmakers investigate the late convicted ⁠sex offender’s ties with political and business elites. Staley appeared before the committee in July as part of its investigation into Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell. Transcripts ⁠from the meeting were released on Wednesday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ex-JPMorgan Chase executive shared confidential bank information with Epstein

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Democrat Eric Hafner, to be released in 2036, also ran for seat in 2024, securing spot on that general election ballot
A man who is serving time in a federal prison in New York advanced on Wednesday from the primary for Alaska’s lone US House seat.
Eric Hafner, a registered Democrat, also ran for the seat in 2024 and secured a spot on the general election ballot that November despite a challenge brought by the Alaska Democratic party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man in prison in New York advances in primary for Alaska’s US House seat

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
Then House candidate joined Democratic Socialists of America in 2018 but didn’t renew membership after a year
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America after not renewing her membership for seven years, amid speculation that she might run for president in 2028.
The 36-year-old New York representative and one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists renewed her membership in the group’s national organization after reports emerged earlier this month that it had lapsed. Ocasio-Cortez initially joined the group in 2018.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez rejoins DSA after membership lapse of seven years

articles.author: Rachel Leingang
articles.description:
LaMonica McIver, a Democrat from New Jersey, was charged with interfering with an arrest in May 2025 at ICE facility
A federal appeals court has declined to dismiss criminal charges against a sitting US congresswoman who visited an immigration facility as part of congressional oversight.
LaMonica McIver, a Democrat who represents New Jersey’s 10th congressional district, was charged with interfering with an arrest in May 2025 outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility that has drawn protests over poor conditions inside.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Federal appeals court declines to dismiss criminal charges against US congresswoman

articles.author: Robert Reich
articles.description:
They should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’
The midterm elections are already upon us, and every Democrat and independent running against a Republican should ask voters the question Ronald Reagan asked on 28 October 1980, at the end of his televised debate against Jimmy Carter: “Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?”
Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”
Energy bills have increased three times faster than the rate of inflation while Trump has been president. The national average monthly utility bill reached $280 in early 2026, a 12% increase since the end of 2024, just before the second Trump administration took office.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November | Robert Reich

articles.author: Ted Widmer
articles.description:
The quiet-spoken Canadian prime minister has spoken unutterable truths
Is it perhaps a sign of the times that Mark Carney, the prime minister of Canada, has become a thrilling orator? A sober banker, he speaks calmly, without many vocal inflections. We expect Canadians to be somewhat flat; even a little boring, and yet Carney has already delivered two remarkable speeches in 2026, and the year is far from over.
The first, at Davos, described a “rupture in the world order”, and “the end of a pleasant fiction”. By that, he meant that the world could no longer depend on the United States to lead the Pax Americana that has largely kept the peace since the end of the second world war.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Mark Carney’s speeches have become political earthquakes | Ted Widmer

articles.author: Rafael Behr
articles.description:
Everyone can see that the Iran war has been a strategic disaster for the US, while a failing president pretends he is winning
Now is the twilight of Donald Trump’s supremacy. The US is still the richest and most heavily armed nation on Earth. That status is secure. The current president, contemptuous of law and indulged in lawlessness by a supine Congress, enjoys even greater power than the constitution allows.
With those advantages it takes a special talent for incompetence to look as thwarted and impotent as Trump does with more than two years of his second term still to run.
Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist
 Continue reading...
articles.title: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael Behr

articles.author: Kenneth Rogoff
articles.description:
With the federal deficit near 6% of GDP and the national debt over $40tn, America’s fiscal position looks increasingly precarious

Bessent ‘will lose’ battle with bond markets, ex-mentor warns

Are we seeing the first signs of panic in Donald Trump’s Treasury? The US is by far the world’s biggest debtor, and the steady rise in global long-term interest rates – which I have long argued was inevitable – is starting to cause real pain.
Until now, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has dismissed concerns about US debt, which recently surpassed $40tn, as a big nothingburger. Growth, in his telling, will be so spectacular the US will easily be able to meet its interest obligations without any significant tax rises or spending cuts, while the rest of the world will happily keep feeding it money. But if Bessent really believes that, why is he trying to strong-arm the bond market by fiddling with the maturity structure of government debt?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is the Trump Treasury panicking over the level of US debt?

articles.author: Chris Stein
articles.description:
Adam Hamilton, a liberal megachurch pastor, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall in this year’s midterm election
In one of the first ads of his campaign to represent Kansas in the US Senate, the Democrat Adam Hamilton stands grilling steaks at a barbecue and attacks his opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, for supporting “tariffs and war”.
If history is any guide, it is Hamilton who is set to get cooked. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close. But he and his supporters believe circumstances have conspired to end this streak – and potentially deliver Democrats control of the Senate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?

articles.author: Roque Planas in Comstock, Texas
articles.description:
The president’s border wall plan could damage or destroy ‘the oldest-known books in North America’
On an overcast summer morning, Carolyn Boyd, an archeologist at Texas State University, stood at the foot of a cave in west Texas, looking up toward a series of towering murals painted on a rock wall. Three massive human-like figures soared toward an overhang that had sheltered the painting from the elements since they were drawn here perhaps 4,000 years ago.
An artist herself, Boyd knows how hard it would have been to paint these long, crisp lines. Before starting, the bands of Indigenous hunter-gatherers who lived in this west Texas valley, where the Pecos River empties into the Rio Grande, would have spent weeks pulverizing gypsum, hematite, limonite and manganese to make paint. They would have gathered massive quantities of sotol stalks to fold its fibers into scaffolding. The painting itself would have required teamwork and precision, with people at the bottom guiding artists on the wall as they painted figures stretching up to 30ft tall.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s border wall construction threatens rock art as old as the pyramids: ‘The ancestors are still here’

articles.author: Chris Stein in Marshall, North Carolina
articles.description:
The Democratic and the Republican candidate each blame the other for the bungled recovery effort after storm struck region
Two years after North Carolina suffered the worst natural disaster in its history when Hurricane Helene struck the state’s western half, life in the hardest-hit areas appears back to normal. Downtowns are lively, blocked roads have been reopened and rivers are flowing below their banks.
But the telltale evidence of the disaster’s expensive impacts can still be seen – from “for rent” signs in storefronts whose businesses never came back to debris from the storm still lurking in some waterways. And in the race for North Carolina’s US Senate seat, it’s almost as if the hurricane never left.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Devastation, doubt and blame: Hurricane Helene looms over North Carolina’s US Senate race

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
US president, pushing on with Freedom 250 festivities, makes over nation’s capital for Trump rally on wheels

Kyle Kirkwood wins Freedom 250 IndyCar race after Trump waves the green flag

He got the wrong end of the stick. Donald Trump couldn’t figure out how to hold the green flag until his wife, Melania Trump, and Command Sgt Maj Matt Williams set him right. Then the US president waved the flag fast and furious like an excited schoolboy. The race was under way – and his conquest of Washington DC was complete.
Since returning to Washington, Trump has deployed the national guard, wrecked the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, demolished the East Wing of the White House and run the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts into the ground. His face adorns the Department of Justice, and he still has grand plans for a triumphal arch worthy of a Roman emperor.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Start your engines! Trump completes fast and furious takeover of Washington with IndyCar race

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Paul Owen ; produced by Bryony Moore ; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
articles.description:
One of Donald Trump’s closest and most devoted aides, Natalie Harp, has faced intense media scrutiny this week, after a Democratic senator, Jon Ossoff, name-checked her in a speech that went viral. So what do we know about Harp, who is often referred to as the ‘human printer’? And why is everybody talking about her relationship with Trump? Helen Pidd speaks to international news editor Paul Owen
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why is Trump’s ‘human printer’ aide Natalie Harp suddenly in the spotlight? - The Latest

articles.author: Jonathan Freedland with Jill Lepore . Produced by Nada Smiljanic, and Danielle Stephens
articles.description:
Less than three months to go until the midterms, voters are thinking about grocery prices, the Iran war and… datacentres.

This week, Jonathan Freedland speaks to historian Jill Lepore about how this latest AI backlash could influence those all-important elections in November. Are we seeing the beginning of the end of the 'artificial state'?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Historian Jill Lepore on the datacentre backlash | Politics Weekly America

articles.description:
The US president waxed lyrical about grass being added around the new White House helipad in front of the media. 'You know, grass has a life like humans have a life,' Trump said
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump talks about grass as he shows off White House renovations – video

articles.author: Presented by Jonathan Freedland with Tara Setmayer; produced by Danielle Stephens and Nada Smiljanic . The executive producer was Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
When Air Force One took off from Turkey after July’s Nato summit, almost everyone believed Donald Trump was on board … but he wasn’t. Jonathan Freedland talks to Tara Setmayer of the Seneca Project about why the White House felt the need to come up with such an elaborate lie to protect the president
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s great plane escape | Politics Weekly America

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose
articles.description:
Government measures to improve resilience are not due until 2030 and July’s  hack has not altered this timeline
 
Hundreds of Britain’s smallest power plants could remain at a higher risk to state-sponsored cyber-attacks until the 2030s despite a successful Iran-linked hack last month, it has emerged.
Officials this week briefed energy bosses on the breach, which is understood to have shut an unnamed small gas power plant for four days last month, and put the industry on alert over the growing cyber threat facing energy infrastructure.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK’s small power plants face continued cyber risk after Iran-linked hack

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Report shines light on ‘catastrophic situation’ where young people make themselves more ill to avoid losing support
Some of the most vulnerable children and young people in care are deliberately self-harming to avoid being abandoned when they get better or turn 18 and face a “cliff edge” of no further support, according to research.
Abi Booth, a psychotherapist who works with children and young people, said some were in a “catastrophic situation” in which they were hurting themselves to keep their place in therapeutic facilities.
In the UK, the youth suicide charity Papyrus can be contacted on 0800 068 4141 or email pat@papyrus-uk.org, and in the UK and Ireland Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is at 988 or chat for support. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Vulnerable children deliberately self-harming to stay in care, research finds

articles.description:
Tim Curry was a versatile performer of stage and screen who made his name as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show. Curry’s best-known roles often required a considerable physical transformation, to the extent that he was unrecognisable in some of them. As Frank-N-Furter, Rocky Horror’s eccentric scientist, he was daubed in garish makeup and dressed in stockings and suspenders Ridley Scott's fantasy Legend, he sported giant horns and scarlet skin as the Lord of Darkness and, in 1990, Curry was transformed with full-face clown makeup to play Pennywise in the TV miniseries It, based on Stephen King's novel


Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tim Curry, the prolific performer who transformed for the screen – video

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime
The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.
Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
articles.description:
Rules will require hedge funds, insurers and pension firms to report all non-financial wrongdoing  
The City’s largest hedge funds, insurers and pension funds are racing to prepare for sweeping rules that will stop nearly 40,000 companies from hiding bullying and harassment cases from the financial watchdog.
From the start of next month, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will expand a crackdown on bad behaviour in the banking industry to a wider group of City investment firms and brokers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: City firms race to prepare for FCA crackdown on bullying and harassment

articles.author: Sandra Laville Environment correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: utility company wants to draw off tens of millions of litres of water a day from Thames and replace it with treated effluent
Levels of a toxic “forever chemical” rose to 13 times the legal limit during Thames Water pilots for a controversial multimillion pound water recycling scheme that will pump millions of litres of treated sewage into the River Thames during drought.
The data from the pilots is in stark contrast to public comments from Thames Water that their water recycling project in south-west London will not harm the riverine environment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Forever chemicals’ surge during pilot of Thames Water plan to combat drought

articles.author: Helena Horton and George Francis Lee
articles.description:
Horticulturalists begin moving and propagating plants before the rusty and warped Palm House begins renovation – but some are too tall to save
It will be a gut-wrenching moment for the horticulturalists at Kew Gardens when some of the magnificent trees in the Palm House have to be felled.
“There are some sad moments ahead,” said Palm House manager, Will Spoelstra, who knows all the plants inside the cathedral-like greenhouse.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Sad moments ahead’: Kew Gardens to fell rare trees in race to save Victorian greenhouse

articles.author: Chris Osuh
articles.description:
Allegations Nathan Cofnas was unqualified for Ghent role and would cause ‘negative impact’ made to senior leaders months ago
Nathan Cofnas, the academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism, has been accused of having “very limited expertise” for his academic role by professors also working at Ghent University, who say he has a “far-right agenda”.
Cofnas secured a postdoctoral research role “on the future of liberalism” at Belgium’s Ghent University in March. Weeks later, Ghent’s department of philosophy and moral sciences handed a 19-page statement to university officials, setting out why it believed it was “improbable” that Cofnas was the best candidate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ghent professors challenged expertise of Jason Arday’s plagiarism accuser

articles.author: Matthew Pearce
articles.description:
Findings from research into illnesses associated with bathing in lakes and rivers come amid boom in hobby
Wild swimming has been linked to a higher risk of stomach bugs and skin rashes, according to the largest ever controlled study of illnesses associated with bathing in rivers and lakes.
The research found that swimmers at locations in Hungary were more than twice as likely to develop skin problems, while the risk of contracting a stomach bug rose significantly in water with higher concentrations of E coli and other bacteria linked to faecal pollution.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wild swimming linked to higher risk of stomach bugs and skin rashes

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Parliamentary committee welcomes fact most of 472 missing have been found but ‘extremely concerned’ for rest
Forty children who went missing from hotels housing asylum seekers in the UK have still not been found, according to a parliamentary report.
Ministers are facing calls from MPs and peers to explain what they are doing to locate the group, two of whom are believed to still be under 18. The figure emerged in a report on Thursday by the joint committee on human rights on how the social care system is failing young adults.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Forty children reported missing from UK asylum hotels still not found

articles.author: Robyn Vinter
articles.description:
The 80-seat venue at Edinburgh fringe combines sauna rituals with theatre, music, storytelling … and sweat
Tucked away behind the Summerhall arts centre is the hottest new venue at the Edinburgh fringe … quite literally. The Sauna theatre has proved popular among theatregoers at the world’s largest performing arts festival, with shows inside its purpose-built, 80-seat sauna drawing sweaty, swimwear-clad crowds.
Visitors may be forgiven for thinking the sauna is a gimmick, especially at the fringe where absurd, experimental and ludicrous performances are not uncommon. This year they include a man drinking his own urine, someone singing the same song over and over, physical feats of exertion and several fully naked shows.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hot ticket: UK’s first sauna theatre draws swimwear-clad audiences

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided
Neurosurgeons in London have performed the world’s first successful AI-assisted operation to remove a brain tumour, saving the sight of a 48-year-old man, health officials have said.
The surgery was performed in May at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (NHNN), part of University College London hospitals NHS foundation trust, but details were kept secret until Thursday while the patient, Rhys Hibbert, recovered.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: London neurosurgeons perform first successful AI-assisted operation to remove brain tumour

articles.author: Heather Stewart
articles.description:
Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way
Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme.
He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
DIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricity

Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills?

Plug-in solar panels will go on sale in the UK for the first time from Thursday, allowing households unable to use rooftop panels to also generate their own cheap electricity.
Households across the country will be able to join the millions across mainland Europe who generate their own renewable electricity using “balcony solar panels”, which will be stocked by some of the UK’s biggest retailers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Plug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first time

articles.author: Kiran Stacey Policy editor
articles.description:
PM said he would set bar at £500k, but trade unions say funding reforms could undermine their ability to donate to Labour
Andy Burnham has dropped his support for capping political donations, causing anger among activists and Labour MPs who have long campaigned for change to the way parties are funded.
The prime minister has decided not to back amendments to the elections bill, which would cap the amount a person or an organisation can give in a single donation, according to government sources.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donors

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Streeting says role is chance to show strength and challenge stereotype that ‘persists in dark corners of internet’
Wes Streeting has described receiving a mass of homophobic abuse since he was made defence secretary last month, while also saying his appointment had been welcomed by some in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) as a sign of change.
Until 2000, gay men and lesbian women were banned from serving in the UK military, with about 200-plus personnel thrown out of the forces each year due to their sexuality – an estimate, as proper records were not kept.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wes Streeting describes ‘unbelievable volume’ of homophobic abuse since becoming defence secretary

articles.author: Laura Snapes
articles.description:
Insecure Men singer has now been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations about his behaviour
Saul Adamczewski of Insecure Men and formerly of Fat White Family has been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations of physical and emotional abuse against the musician.
One woman said that the pair had a short relationship that resulted in a pregnancy, after which, she alleged, Adamczewski “made it his duty to make me suffer. He has been violent, pushed me, thrown glass bottles at me, showered me with beer […] insulted me, taken my passport from me, stolen my money and more, all while I had our baby.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two women accuse former Fat White Family member Saul Adamczewski of physical and emotional abuse

articles.author: Ben Quinn and Amelia Casey-Rerhaye
articles.description:
Reform MP seeks to heap pressure on Tory leader amid confusion around details of meeting with Giorgia Meloni
Robert Jenrick has accused Kemi Badenoch of telling “a pack of lies” about her meeting with the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, as he launched a deeply personal attack on his former boss.
The Reform UK MP sought to heap pressure on the Conservative leader amid confusion about whether Meloni urged Badenoch at a meeting in Rome to “be her own woman” and resist doing a deal with his party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Pack of lies’: Robert Jenrick launches personal attack on Kemi Badenoch

articles.author: Taz Ali (now) and Martin Belam (earlier)
articles.description:
Prime minister spoke to press while on visit to a Sainsbury’s supermarket in London this morning
Over 40,000 more people died on the hottest days in England between 1988 and 2025 than would be expected, according to data published by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday.
The figures do not include this summer, when England has sweltered under a succession of heatwaves and is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone. The total is almost double the figure for the whole summer in 2025.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK politics: Burnham announces plan for 10,000 work experience placements for young people – as it happened

articles.author: Rob Davies
articles.description:
Sentiment in hospitality and brewing sectors more positive since business rates action, trade bodies’ survey finds
Pubs, bars and hotels have reported a “Burnham bounce” in optimism as a result of the prime minister’s overtures to the sector, polling suggests, but they warn that the goodwill could evaporate without further tax relief.
Andy Burnham has positioned himself as a staunch ally of the UK’s hospitality industry both before and since his arrival at No 10, announcing last month a discount on business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pubs, bars and hotels report ‘Burnham bounce’ in optimism but call for further tax relief

articles.author: Hannah Devlin Science correspondent
articles.description:
Scientists found those who had used hormone replacement therapy were 10% less likely to be diagnosed with dementia
Hormone replacement therapy may reduce the risk of dementia, a study has found.
Scientists tracked more than 180,000 postmenopausal women in the UK in the largest study of its kind. They found that those who had used HRT were 10% less likely to develop any type of dementia and 16% less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, the most common form, compared with those who had never used it.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Women using HRT at lower risk of dementia, study suggests

articles.author: Tara Conlan
articles.description:
To Nicola, Love Peter will focus on couple’s relationship during 12-year period of embezzlement and fallout of case
Channel 5 is reuniting with the producers of Power: the Downfall of Huw Edwards for a drama about how Nicola Sturgeon’s estranged husband embezzled £400,000 from the Scottish National party and the impact it had on her reputation.
To Nicola, Love Peter will examine the couple’s relationship over the 12-year period that Peter Murrell diverted funds from the SNP while he was the chief executive to spend on items including a £124,550 motorhome and more than £2,600 on a pair of luxury salt and pepper grinders.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Channel 5 drama to examine how Nicola Sturgeon’s estranged husband stole SNP funds

articles.author: Damian Carrington Environment editor
articles.description:
ONS data shows rising toll of climate crisis, with officials warning this summer on track to set further records
More than 40,000 extra people died on the hottest days in England between 1988 and 2025 than would be expected in normal temperatures, according to data published by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday.
The figures do not include this summer, when England has sweltered under a succession of heatwaves and is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone. The total is almost double the figure for the whole summer in 2025.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘National scandal’: extreme heat linked to 40,000 deaths in England between 1988 and 2025

articles.author: Mark Sweney
articles.description:
Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year

Business live – latest updates

The rollout of robotaxis on the streets of London is unlikely to happen this year, as regulatory and technical hurdles push back the ambitious schedule set out by the UK government.
Only weeks ago Uber and London-based Wayve were granted the first minicab licences in the capital to allow them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now – and said they would start trips “later this summer” before a full public launch.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: London rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to follow

articles.author: Damien Gayle Environment correspondent
articles.description:
Civil society groups argue climate crisis means transport sector needs to urgently reduce its carbon emissions
Dozens of civil society groups have demanded the UK government do more to promote cycling and walking, after this summer’s extreme heat exposed the desperate need to decarbonise transport.
This summer’s heatwaves and wildfires were “immediate, real-world manifestations of the climate emergency”, the groups said, making reform of transport – responsible for more carbon emissions than any other sector in the UK – an urgent priority.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Heatwaves show UK must do more to promote cycling and walking, campaigners say

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
A typical household in Great Britain will pay £1,723 a year, prompting calls for more support

Nils Pratley: Labour’s energy bills crisis is getting worse


Millions of British households will face the highest energy charges in three years this winter after months of rising market prices pushed up the government’s price cap for the second time in three months.
Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from October under the new cap, after climbing 13% at the start of July to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the war on Iran.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Britons face highest price cap in three years as energy bills rise 4% from October

articles.author: Sarah Marsh Consumer affairs correspondent
articles.description:
NHS ombudsman warns of years-long waits and patients paying thousands to go private as demand for services soars
Complaints about autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder services in England have more than tripled in five years, official figures show, with the NHS ombudsman warning of years-long waits and patients paying thousands of pounds for private care.
One woman was removed from an ADHD medication waiting list without warning after almost four years, leaving her without the support she needed for about six months. Another patient was given an autism assessment lasting just 50 minutes that failed to follow guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, while a man referred to an ADHD service that was not yet operational ended up paying almost £4,000 for private treatment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Autism and ADHD care complaints more than triple in five years in England

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Despite the policy not being included in the party’s 2024 manifesto, Andy Burnham is under pressure to act 
Andy Burnham is facing new pressure to act over electoral reform, with nearly 100 of his MPs backing a commission to decide on a route to replace the first-past-the-post voting system. Why is this an issue for Labour – and will anything happen?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

articles.author: Isaaq Tomkins
articles.description:
Robert Corrigan has been dealing with the ‘smart’ rodents all his life – and believes there are better solutions to deal with the growing infestation in the world’s cities
“The rodents have paid for every single bill I’ve ever had – every mortgage, every car payment, every pint of Guinness,” says Dr Robert Corrigan. “It’s been a great ride and I’m still at it.”
New York-based Corrigan is one of the most respected voices in the world of rodentology. Now in his 70s, he has devoted his entire adult life to studying rats and our relationship with them.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I love rats but we can’t live with them’: the headache of rising rodent populations around the world

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running
The carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed.
Experts have said this demonstrates the “serious threat” datacentres pose to the UK’s legally binding climate goals.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis finds

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
NHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screening
Millions of women in England who have missed cervical screening appointments will be offered free home testing kits on the NHS.
The move comes amid concerns that only two-thirds of women attend in-person cervical screening appointments when asked to do so, leaving as many as 4 million women not up to date.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS England to offer women ‘gamechanging’ free home testing kits for cervical cancer

articles.author: Luke Harding and Dan Sabbagh in Pavlohrad, Ukraine
articles.description:
As well as pledging military help and diplomatic backing, the prime minister could be useful in dealing with the US
Since moving into Downing Street in July, Andy Burnham – a foreign policy neophyte – has expressed strong support for Ukraine. But on Monday he saw the bitter human cost of the war up close for the first time, visiting Kyiv during his first international trip as prime minister.
The occasion was the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave awards to the families of fallen soldiers. Relatives wept, hugging Ukraine’s president. Photos of young men in their prime were shown on a giant screen.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for Ukraine

articles.author: Sam Jones
articles.description:
EU police agency says shift could point to involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific artefacts
Robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way into buildings and display cases, according to a report by Europol.
The EU police agency said that while museum thefts were generally seen as a non-violent form of organised property crime, member states had detected a recent shift “towards violent and forceful methods” that could point to the involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific cultural artefacts.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Guns, axes, explosives: violent museum heists are on the rise, says Europol

articles.author: Kiran Stacey Policy editor
articles.description:
PM’s honeymoon period will come to an end as he makes decisions on the budget, welfare, migration and prisons
Andy Burnham has enjoyed a month-long honeymoon period since he became prime minister, winning public support with a series of popular but relatively low-cost announcements. They have included cutting VAT on electricity bills, reducing the cost of bus travel and reviewing business rates for small businesses.
But as MPs prepare to return to the Commons in just over a week, the prime minister is about to face his first real challenge in office, as he makes a number of key decisions that could create enemies but define his premiership.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to Commons

articles.author: Rajeev Syal and Faisa Mohamed
articles.description:
Treatment is already required by parole boards in several countries, but some feel the practice is unethical

Thousands of sex offenders in England and Wales could get libido-suppressing drugs

For some prisoners with problematic sexual arousal (PSA), “images of sex flood their minds” all of their waking hours, according to Prof Belinda Winder, a leading forensic psychologist who has evaluated the use of drugs to control libidos.
“I remember talking to one guy a few weeks after he started taking the medication. He said: ‘It’s amazing. I followed a film plot. I wasn’t just looking for when I could see bra straps, when I could see nipples, when someone’s going to bend over so I could see their bum.”
